title: Riemannian metrics, coordinate expressions and coordinate singularities
summary: Conventions (signature, index placement, summation); the definition of a Riemannian metric and arc length; metric coefficients in a chart and the transformation law under change of coordinates; induced metrics computed from a parametrisation and the ambient inner product; the Gram criterion separating coordinate singularities from geometric ones; isometries, conformal maps, homogeneous spaces and local orthonormal frames; existence of metrics via partitions of unity; the Lorentzian case named and kept apart.

objectives.description: State the definition of a Riemannian metric with the conventions (signature, index placement, Einstein summation) and compute arc lengths.
Derive the metric coefficients of a submanifold of Euclidean space from a parametrisation, including the sphere of radius R in spherical coordinates, and identify the chart domain.
Prove the transformation law of the metric coefficients and its consequences for the determinant and positive definiteness, and explain a coordinate singularity via the Gram criterion.
Define isometries and conformal maps, recognise the round sphere as a homogeneous space, and state which constructions of the unit survive in Lorentzian signature.

preparation.description: Read Gudmundsson chapter 5, p. 63: Definition 5.5 (Riemannian metric), Example 5.6 (Euclidean space), Definition 5.7 (arc length).
Read p. 64: Example 5.8 (the punctured round sphere), Example 5.9 (hyperbolic ball), Proposition 5.10 (distance function); then p. 65: Definition 5.11 (induced metric) and Example 5.12.
Read pp. 66–67: Fact 5.15 and Theorem 5.16 (existence of metrics), Definition 5.17 (conformal, isometric, isometry), Example 5.21 (the sphere is homogeneous).
Read p. 71: Remark 5.30 (pull-back metric in a parametrisation) and Example 5.32 (coordinate and orthonormal frames); glance at Exercise 5.2 (p. 74) after attempting exercise 1.
Optional, if you have the book: Lee, chapter 2 (Riemannian Metrics), including the section on pseudo-Riemannian metrics for exercise 3. Commercial reference; not required.

exitCheck.description: Exercise 1 accepted: the chart domain identified; g_θθ = R², g_θφ = 0, g_φφ = R² sin²θ derived from the ambient inner product with conventions stated; the pole analysed as a coordinate singularity with a second chart showing g positive definite there; the lengths of a parallel and a meridian arc computed.

commonMisconceptions.claim: The metric of the sphere is singular at the poles because g_φφ = R² sin²θ vanishes there.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The vanishing is a property of the spherical-coordinate parametrisation, which is not an immersion at θ = 0, π (the whole φ-segment collapses to a point). In a graph or stereographic chart the metric coefficients at the pole form a positive definite matrix. The Gram criterion makes this precise: det(g_ij) → 0 exactly where the parametrisation loses rank.

commonMisconceptions.claim: det(g_ij) is a function on the manifold.
commonMisconceptions.correction: It transforms by the square of the Jacobian determinant under change of chart, so it is a density, not a function; only its combination with dx¹…dxⁿ is chart-independent.

commonMisconceptions.claim: A Lorentzian metric is a Riemannian metric with one sign changed, so everything in this unit applies.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Positive definiteness is used in the arc-length formula, in the distance function (Proposition 5.10) and in the existence proof via convex combinations (Theorem 5.16); each fails or needs modification in signature (−,+,+,+). The transformation law and the invertibility of (g_ij) do carry over.

commonMisconceptions.claim: An isometry is any smooth map preserving the metric tensor.
commonMisconceptions.correction: An isometric map preserves g (it is then an immersion); an isometry is additionally a diffeomorphism. Stereographic projection restricted to the punctured sphere is an isometry onto the conformal model, not onto Euclidean space.
